title: An Interview with our CEO: Engineering Confidence into Critical Power
summary: Ultralife CEO Mike Manna discusses battery safety, custom power solutions, and innovation in defense, medical and other mission-critical markets.
body_markdown:
When a battery powers a[medical device](https://ultralifecorporation.com/industries/commercial-medical/) ,[defense application](https://ultralifecorporation.com/industries/government-defense/) , or[equipment deep underground](https://ultralifecorporation.com/industries/oil-and-gas/) , reliability is more than a specification. It determines whether a product performs when needed.[Ultralife Corporation](https://ultralifecorporation.com/) engineers power solutions for customers who cannot treat batteries as interchangeable commodities.


Headquartered in the United States, Ultralife manufactures[Lithium cells, battery packs](https://ultralifecorporation.com/custom-capabilities/npd-process/) and develops[communications](https://ultralifecorporation.com/communication-systems/) and related technical systems. Its roots reach back to the late 1980s, when it emerged from Kodak’s power division as Kodak shifted its focus toward film. Publicly traded since the early 1990s, it also draws on acquired businesses dating to the 1950s and 1970s. It serves specialized markets including[defense](https://ultralifecorporation.com/industries/government-defense/) ,[medical technology](https://ultralifecorporation.com/industries/commercial-medical/) , and[oil and gas](https://ultralifecorporation.com/industries/oil-and-gas/) , where unreliable power can cost time, money, equipment, or lives.


Ultralife primarily manufactures non-rechargeable lithium cells while exploring select rechargeable chemistries for[custom projects](https://ultralifecorporation.com/custom-capabilities/npd-process/) and potential future opportunities. Its experience with lithium-metal chemistry gives the company a detailed understanding of the safety and performance considerations shaping both cells and finished packs. Rather than relying solely on supplier datasheets, its teams consider how chemistry, electronics, packaging, and operating conditions interact. That technical depth defines Ultralife’s value proposition: engineer the right solution for an application, test it thoroughly, and plan for its long-term use. “Our number one priority is always safety. Safety informs cell selection, pack design, validation, manufacturing, and regulatory compliance. The aim is to remove energy and power as a source of uncertainty over the entire product life cycle,” says[Mike Manna](https://ultralifecorporation.com/about-us/leadership/) , President & CEO, Ultralife Corporation.


The company uses thousands of test channels to evaluate cells and packs. Most of its rechargeable packs are tested in full before shipment. Component-level traceability supports the rigors of medical device traceability and for defense customers operating in extreme conditions, knowing the origin and technical maturity provides an assurance that the power system will function when called upon. Over the years, Ultralife has developed working relationships with accredited regulatory testing bodies to support launch of products globally. The company and its technical experts have been called upon by safety and regulatory bodies to provide input and support the development of lithium battery safety standards.


Customer collaboration often begins before the design is settled. A client may know what a device should do without a specification that reflects real-world constraints. Ultralife engineers help define achievable requirements, balancing energy and power density, runtime, size, temperature tolerance, charging, industrial design, human factors, safety under abuse conditions and above all reliable repeatable manufacturability. A medical device intended for a hospital may later be deployed in an aircraft, a military unit, or a mobile environment where conditions are less controlled. Anticipating those possibilities can prevent expensive problems. Ultralife products are engineered to fulfill the rigors of the application, with margins that allow the design to be ported to adjacent applications - safely.


A ruggedized underground application illustrates the value of early collaboration. The customer needed a compact, high-voltage battery pack able to withstand temperature extremes and accommodate unusual communication requirements. Its original specification was too broad to design against. Across nine iterations and nearly two and a half to three months of specification development work, Ultralife and the customer reconciled requirements with the capabilities of available chemistries, cells, and electronics. The program ultimately succeeded. Not every brief is feasible as first imagined. Manna described the discipline involved: “We’re dealing with physics most of the time. Rather than promise performance that technology cannot deliver, Ultralife clarifies trade-offs and, when necessary, helps customers reconsider specifications or functionality.” The company invests in preliminary engineering even when it does not win the contract, recognizing that a realistic specification is the foundation of a dependable product.


Lithium packs face mechanical requirements for vibration and temperature cycling, while demanding applications may require additional tests. Design revisions can trigger retesting and costs. Component obsolescence adds another challenge: a product may need to remain in service long after original parts become difficult to source. Medical devices can operate for eight to twelve years and need spare-parts support afterward. Ultralife works with suppliers to track the availability road maps for components such as MOSFETs, fuel gauges, and fuses, helping customers limit redesigns and interruptions. Moreover, their long-standing relationships and responsive support reinforce the engineering offer. Some customer relationships span more than 30 years. Ultralife aims to be an indispensable partner, even recommending another supplier when a commodity solution is not a fit for its specialist capabilities. Technical resources across nearly every continent provide local support. “Our goal is to be the first call they make on portable power requirements,” Manna adds.


Jeff Luke, Chief Marketing Officer, has described the culture behind the company in a public post about returning to Ultralife: “We are a technology company with a global footprint, centers of excellence, and multiple brands—but there is a human element at work here that holds us all together.” The observation reflects Ultralife’s emphasis on collaboration and sustained customer engagement.


Today, Ultralife is pursuing new cell chemistries, manufacturing methods, and packaging approaches, with miniaturization a particular focus in medical wearables. The company is working toward a patent pending non-rechargeable cell less than one millimeter thick while continuing to explore rechargeable technologies. It is also considering opportunities linked to U.S. manufacturing and defense supply-chain requirements, alongside battery-pack applications for underwater, aerial, and land-based drones. Also on product and solutions roadmaps are higher voltage, higher capacity systems to support the ever growing need for portable, reliable, rugged systems that can deliver variable power from stackable energy storage modules. Multi-year customer and supplier agreements improve demand visibility, help secure components, and align production. Its[communications systems](https://ultralifecorporation.com/communication-systems/) business adds another dimension, developing wearable and edge-computing applications for defense and industrial workers. These systems could let technicians access computing and testing tools while being completely disconnected. As batteries become integral to more devices and specialized systems, Ultralife intends to expand selectively. Its value lies not simply in the cell or pack, but in the engineering judgment, rigorous testing, traceability, lifecycle planning, and customer partnership that make dependable power possible.
